newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: NATIONALS SET TO BACK PM'S WIK SOLUTION
The Queensland National Party President, David Russell, says if the Prime Minister's plan for native title delivers certainty for pastoral leases, the Nationals will support it.
Mr Howard's 10-point plan stops short of legislative extinguishment, demanded by the National Party, National Farmers' Federation and some state governments.
A Government source says Mr Howard's plan will give pastoralists the certainty they need and amounts to effective extinguishment of native title on pastoral leases.
It would also avoid the likelihood of a High Court challenge, and increase the chances of the package getting the support of the Senate.
Mr Russell says the package has to deliver extinguishment and his Party is not hung up about the form of the word, only the result.
GOVT MAY BACK SENATE INQUIRY INTO COLSTON
The Government leader in the Senate, Robert Hill, is leaving the door open for a Senate Inquiry into whether Mal Colston and one of his staff misled the Upper House.

Until now the Federal Government has rejected Opposition calls for a Senate Inquiry, arguing this could prejudice the Federal Police investigation into alleged travel rorts by the Independent Senator.
The Clerk of the Senate, Harry Evans, says a Senate inquiry would not jeopardise the police investigation or any court case, and it's important to deal with any untruthful statements to Parliament.
Senator Hill has told ABC Radio the Senate should stand aside while the police complete their work, but can then take whatever action it likes if it's unhappy.
WELFARE BODY CALLS FOR FREE BANK ACCOUNTS
The Council of Social Service in New South Wales says the finance sector has an obligation to provide high quality services to everybody.
The peak welfare body is calling on government authorities to work for a universal no frills bank account, free of transaction fees.
The Council also wants a public interest test applied to plans to close bank branches.
Council director Gary Moore says the Wallis inquiry into the finance sector is promoting increased consumer choice - but that's futile if consumers can't afford what's available.
He says unlike Stan Wallis, the Council believes the finance sector has a community service obligation.
ABC BOARD WARNS OF MORE CUTS IF FUNDING INADEQUATE
The ABC's board has warned that if it fails to receive adequate funding it will have to cut core services including news, current affairs and state based sport.

A statement issued this morning warns that if the ABC does not receive funding of about 500-million-dollars, as consistently promised by the Federal Government, the organisation will be unable to cover state based community events.
The board warns that domestic radio networks will go and up to 50 percent of regional radio stations will be closed.
Up to seventy hours of local television production could be cut.
POLICE DOORKNOCK IN MELBOURNE AFTER SHOOTING
Homicide Squad detectives have begun door knocking the Box Hill area in Melbourne, as they search for information surrounding the fatal shooting of a man last night.
The 44-year-old was found on the front lawn of a house in Heathfield Rise, Box Hill North.
He'd been shot in the head and chest.
Detectives have started door knocking the neighborhood and also plan to conduct a line search of the area. - - - -
CARR WORRIED ABOUT CUTS TO FILM FUNDING
New South Wales Premier Bob Carr has told the Prime Minister Australia will not be able to produce films of the calibre of Shine and Babe if rumoured Budget cuts go ahead.

Mr Carr claims the Federal Government is about cut 140-million-dollars in funding assistance for the film industry. He's appealed to Prime Minister John Howard to maintain the present level of assistance to the industry.
Mr Carr says he's concerned New South Wales' rapidly-growing film industry would suffer most from the cuts.

He says his government has provided increased funding for the film industry including money to establish the Young Film makers Fund, and scored a huge win in attracting Fox Studios over interstate competition.
PROTEST RALLY AGAINST AIRPORT AT HOLSWORTHY
A protest rally of two-thousand people has been given ten reasons why the building of an airport at Holsworthy, south-west of Sydney, should be opposed.

Former ALP minister and head of the Illawarra Against Holsworthy Airport group, Robert Tickner, listed a series of arguments against an airport at the site - including air and noise pollution, the loss of coal reserves worth 40-billion dollars, and clearing tonnes of unexploded shells.
As well, he said the prohibition of hang-gliding at nearby Stanwell Park would damage Sydney's international reputation in the sport.
Mr Tickner says choosing Holsworthy as a potential airport site is planning madness.
He says it would need an engineering project of similar size to the the snowy mountains scheme, and the area includes hundreds of Aboriginal sites.
